subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The No-Hair Theorem
description: A 60-second lesson on The No-Hair Theorem.

hook.text: A black hole can be fully described by just three properties: mass, spin, and electric charge. Nothing else.

buildup.text: Every other detail about what fell in—its shape, composition, history—is erased. The black hole forgets.

discovery.text: John Wheeler coined the phrase: 'Black holes have no hair.' It means they carry no distinguishing features.

twist.text: This conflicts with quantum mechanics, which says information can never be destroyed. That's the information paradox.

climax.text: Solving this paradox may require merging quantum mechanics and gravity—the holy grail of theoretical physics.

punchline.text: Mass, spin, charge. Everything else is erased. Or is it?

quiz.question: What is the 'no-hair theorem' about black holes?
options: Black holes are fully described by only mass, spin, and charge—all other information is lost
Black holes have no physical surface or boundary
Black holes cannot grow larger once they form

details.summary: The no-hair theorem states that a black hole is completely described by just three properties: mass, electric charge, and spin. All other information about the matter that formed it — composition, shape, history — is lost.
details.whyItMatters: The no-hair theorem means black holes destroy information about their origin. This simplicity conflicts with quantum mechanics, which says information can never be destroyed — creating the information paradox.
takeaways: Black holes are defined by only mass, charge, and spin
All other information about the source matter is erased
This conflicts with quantum mechanics' information preservation

faq.question: Why is it called the 'no-hair' theorem?
faq.answer: Physicist John Wheeler coined the phrase 'black holes have no hair' — meaning they lack distinguishing features beyond mass, charge, and spin. 'Hair' metaphorically represents any extra properties. Two black holes with identical mass, charge, and spin are completely indistinguishable.

faq.question: Has the no-hair theorem been tested?
faq.answer: Gravitational wave observations from merging black holes are beginning to test it. The ringdown signal after a merger should match specific predictions based only on the final black hole's mass and spin. Early results from LIGO/Virgo are consistent with the theorem.
